notes.title: Documentation pilot — clinical charter
notes.content:
Scope: two medical-surgical units, 3B and 4A. De-identified data only until the business-associate agreement executes.

Primary measure: after-hours documentation time per clinician per shift, reported in aggregate only.
Secondary: clinician-reported burden, collected by survey.

Governance gate: 30 April. Production requires clinical safety sign-off from me, a privacy determination, a security decision, and an issued order. I hold exactly one of those four.

notes.title: Governance committee — March minutes
notes.content:
Reviewed the pilot at the eight-week mark.

Decision: continue to the April gate. Two conditions — the session timeout on shared workstations must be resolved, and Unit 4A needs a second training round before its numbers count.

Unrecorded discussion is not minuted and does not leave this room.

notes.title: Unit 3B versus 4A — what the difference actually is
notes.content:
3B is showing an 18% drop in after-hours documentation. 4A is flat.

My read is that this is a training gap, not a product one — 4A went live during a staffing shortage and the second training round was cancelled. Patrick agrees.

This matters commercially to the vendor and I should be careful how much of my reasoning travels. The measure is theirs to see; my interpretation of their product's performance is not something I owe them before the committee has it.

notes.title: Clinical safety review — what I look for
notes.content:
Four questions on any clinical workflow change:
1. Can it produce an order or a note without a clinician's explicit action?
2. Does it change what appears at the point of decision?
3. What happens when it is unavailable mid-shift?
4. Who is accountable for its output when it is wrong?

A vendor that cannot answer 3 and 4 has not thought about clinical use.

notes.title: Session timeout — clinical impact
notes.content: The four-minute timeout on shared workstations is not a nuisance. A clinician loses a partially written note mid-documentation and re-enters it from memory. That is a clinical safety issue, not a usability one, and it is why this is a gate condition rather than a backlog item.

notes.title: What I will not do for a vendor
notes.content:
Twice now their team has asked, in different words, for a sample of real charts to tune against. The answer is no and it is not mine to give even if I wanted to.

I have also been asked which clinicians are the heaviest users. That is individual performance data and it does not leave the governance committee.

notes.title: Clinical governance committee — standing scope
notes.content:
Monthly. Reviews any change that touches clinical decision support, order sets, documentation templates, or alerting.

Agenda is usually four items and runs to six. The overruns are always alert-related.

notes.title: Alert fatigue — the programme nobody funds
notes.content:
Clinicians override 87% of medication alerts. That number has been roughly stable for three years across every published study and ours is no different.

Reducing it means switching alerts off, which requires someone to accept the risk of the one that mattered. Nobody wants to be that signature.

notes.title: Order set review — annual
notes.content:
Two hundred and forty order sets, reviewed on a rolling annual cycle by specialty.

Roughly a fifth are unused. Retiring an unused order set is surprisingly contentious because someone always built it.

notes.title: Documentation burden — the actual literature
notes.content:
Clinicians spend roughly two hours on documentation for every hour of direct care. That is the number behind every informatics business case in the sector.

Worth knowing that the number is stable and that most interventions move it by minutes, not hours.

notes.title: Clinical decision support governance
notes.content:
Anything that changes what appears at the point of decision goes through committee, without exception, including a change that only alters wording.

Wording changes behaviour. That is the whole reason decision support exists.

notes.title: Downtime procedures — the gap
notes.content:
Paper procedures exist. Most staff hired in the last four years have never used them.

The last unplanned downtime lasted forty minutes and the recovery took three hours, almost all of it reconciling what happened on paper.

notes.title: Informatics team — capacity
notes.content:
Two informaticists for a system this size is thin. Kenji carries most of it.

The consequence is not that things break, it is that nothing gets improved unless it is on fire.

notes.title: Clinic — Tuesday and Thursday
notes.content:
Two half-days of general internal medicine. I keep them because a CMIO who does not see patients stops understanding what the systems do to a working day.

They also make me unreachable for four hours twice a week, which colleagues find inconvenient and I do not intend to change.

notes.title: Specialty engagement — who actually turns up
notes.content:
Medicine and surgery engage. Emergency engages when something affects them. Radiology and pathology send apologies.

That pattern determines which specialties get systems that suit them, which is a governance failure dressed as a scheduling one.

notes.title: Research informatics requests
notes.content:
Steady trickle from clinicians wanting data. Most do not have ethics approval and are surprised they need it.

The useful early question is 'is this quality improvement or is it research', because the answer determines everything that follows.

notes.title: New clinical system evaluations — general approach
notes.content:
Four questions on anything: what does it change at the point of decision, what happens when it is unavailable, who is accountable for its output, and what does it cost a clinician per encounter.

Most vendors can answer the first and struggle from there.

notes.title: Clinical governance committee — standing agenda
notes.content: Monthly. Decision log, open safety items, change requests, incident review. Two hours and it always overruns on the third item.

notes.title: Order set review — cycle
notes.content: Two hundred and eleven order sets, reviewed on a two-year cycle. Forty are overdue. An out-of-date order set is a clinical risk that looks like an administrative task, which is why it stays overdue.

notes.title: Alert fatigue — the standing problem
notes.content: Clinicians override 89% of drug interaction alerts. That number has been roughly stable for four years across every system I have worked in. Tuning it is a governance question nobody wants to own because the liability sits with whoever turns an alert off.

notes.title: Clinical documentation improvement programme
notes.content: Separate from the vendor pilot and predates it. Query rates, coding accuracy, and the perennial tension between documenting for care and documenting for billing.

notes.title: My clinic — Tuesday and Thursday mornings
notes.content: Two half-days on the general medical clinic. Non-negotiable and the reason my calendar looks the way it does. It also keeps me credible with the people I am asking to change how they work.

notes.title: Downtime procedures — the last drill
notes.content: Units could not find the paper forms. The forms existed. Nobody had opened the box in two years. That finding was worth more than the rest of the exercise.

notes.title: Physician informatics champions
notes.content: One per service line, nominally. Six of eleven filled. It is unpaid, uncredited, and the people who do it well are the ones who least have time.

notes.title: Mortality and morbidity — informatics contributions
notes.content: Two cases this quarter where documentation or system behaviour was a contributing factor. Both went to M&M. Neither was a system defect exactly; both were a workflow nobody had thought through.

notes.title: Regional CMIO network
notes.content: Quarterly call. Ambient documentation vendors are on everyone's agenda and nobody has taken one to production yet. That is worth knowing and worth not saying to a vendor.

notes.title: Why clinical safety sign-off is separate from IT approval
notes.content: IT approves that something works. Clinical safety approves that it is safe to use in care. A system can be entirely functional and clinically unsafe, and the two reviews ask different questions of different people.

notes.title: Nursing documentation burden
notes.content: Larger than the physician burden and much less studied. The pilot measures physicians because physicians complained loudest, which is a sampling problem in the design that I signed off on.

notes.title: Research governance — informatics requests
notes.content: Four data requests this quarter from clinical researchers. All routed to Privacy and Analytics. My role is confirming clinical validity, not permissibility.

notes.title: Committee membership — who actually decides
notes.content: The committee advises. The decision is mine and I sign it. People consistently believe it is a vote, and it is not, and that matters when a decision is unpopular.

todos.content: Forty minutes down, three hours to recover.

todos.content: Nothing improves unless it is on fire.

todos.content: A governance failure dressed as a scheduling one.

todos.content: 87%. Somebody has to be willing to sign.
